# How to Set Reminders with Alexa on Your Echo for Bills, Birthdays and Errands

> **In short:** You can ask your Echo to remind you of bills, birthdays and errands by saying a task, a day and a time, then check and cancel those reminders later. Reminders only ring if your Echo is online, and the exact features may vary with your Alexa+ access and region.

This guide shows you how to build reminders that repeat, add a heads-up before a big date, and confirm or cancel them when plans change. It's for people who already talk to Alexa on an Echo speaker and want their reminders to work for the rest of the month and year, not just for the next hour.

## Before you start

- An Amazon account, and an Echo device linked to it, with Alexa already answering your voice.
- The Alexa app on your phone, signed in to the same account. You'll use it to review your reminders.
- Alexa+ access. Availability can vary, and it may depend on your region or on a paid plan, so check Amazon's official Alexa+ page for current details.
- About 15 minutes. You already know how to start a conversation, so we'll skip straight to reminders.

## Step 1 — Set a reminder with a task, a day and a time

Say the wake word, then speak one complete sentence that names the task, the day and the time. Speak clearly and pause for a second when you finish. Your Echo's light ring usually lights up to show it's listening. Once it understands you, Alexa replies by voice and the reminder is saved to your account, so it will fire on that day at that time. If the reminder doesn't appear in the Alexa app later, the sentence may have been misheard; try again with fewer words. If your Echo doesn't respond at all, check that it's connected to Wi-Fi and that the mute button isn't on.

💬 Example: "Remind me to call my mom on [day of the week] at [time]."

You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms the reminder out loud and you can see it in the Alexa app's reminders list.

## Step 2 — Make a bill reminder that repeats

Bills come back every month, so the reminder should repeat too. Say the task, the amount of days you want, and the word "every." Alexa's wording for repeating items can differ slightly between versions, so if it asks a follow-up question, answer it with a short phrase like the day of the month. This is the basic repeat pattern: a task, a frequency, and a time. Remember that a reminder is only a nudge; it doesn't pay the bill for you, and it can't see your bank balance. Keep your payment schedule in your own bank or service app.

💬 Example: "Remind me to pay the [utility company] bill every month on the [day number] at [time]."

You'll know it worked when Alexa repeats back the monthly schedule and the reminder shows a repeat in the Alexa app.

## Step 3 — Add an early heads-up for a birthday

A birthday reminder is more useful when it arrives a day early, so you have time to buy a card. Say both moments in one sentence: the birthday date and the earlier reminder. Alexa may create two separate reminders, or one reminder with a lead time, depending on how it parses your words. Either way is fine, as long as you check both in the next step. If Alexa only sets one reminder, say a second sentence that starts with "remind me" and names the earlier day.

💬 Example: "Remind me that [person's name] has a birthday on [month and day], and remind me one day before at [time]."

You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms the birthday reminder and the earlier one appears as a separate entry in the reminders list.

## Step 4 — Check every reminder in the Alexa app

Open the Alexa app on your phone and look for a reminders section. It's often in a menu or under a tab labeled something like "More" or a calendar-style icon, but menu names change, so search the app for the word "reminders" if you can't find it quickly. Scroll through the list and compare each entry to what you meant. Check the task, the day, the time and whether it repeats. If something is missing, say it again to your Echo. If a reminder is wrong, don't worry; the next steps show you how to fix it.

💬 Example: "Show me all of my reminders for this week."

You'll know it worked when you can read each reminder in the app and match it to what you asked for.

## Step 5 — Change a reminder when plans shift

Plans change, so reminders need to change too. Say what you want to move, the old time and the new time. Alexa should confirm the change out loud. Many people find it easier to make the change in a single sentence rather than cancelling and rebuilding. If Alexa asks which reminder you mean, answer with the task name, because it may hear two similar items.

💬 Example: "Move my reminder to [task name] from [old time] to [new time]."

You'll know it worked when the reminder's time in the Alexa app matches your new time.

## Step 6 — Cancel a reminder you no longer need

When an errand is done or a bill has been paid for good, cancel the reminder so it doesn't ring again. Say the task name and ask Alexa to cancel it. For a repeating reminder, Alexa may ask whether you want to cancel just the next one or the whole series, so answer clearly. You can also delete it in the Alexa app's reminders list. If the reminder still rings after you cancel it, close the app, reopen it, and check the list again. Sometimes the app needs a refresh before the change shows up.

💬 Example: "Cancel my reminder to [task name]."

You'll know it worked when the reminder is gone from the Alexa app's list and Alexa confirms the cancellation.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake: saying the task without a day or time.** Alexa may set a vague reminder or ask a question. *Fix:* always end your sentence with a day and a clock time, like "on Friday at 9 a.m."
- **Mistake: cancelling only the next repeat when you meant the whole series.** The bill keeps reminding you forever. *Fix:* when Alexa asks which one you mean, say "all of them" or "the whole series," then check the app.
- **Mistake: assuming Alexa pays bills or tracks deadlines for you.** A reminder is only a nudge, and Alexa can't see your bank account. *Fix:* pay the bill in your bank or service's own app, and use the reminder as a prompt to do it.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** A reminder for the monthly water or internet bill, plus an early heads-up for a family birthday, can save you a late fee and a last-minute gift scramble.
- **For your business or work:** Repeating reminders for weekly errands like supply pickups or a recurring call can keep small tasks from slipping, as long as you check the Alexa app once in a while.
- **If you want to go further:** Try grouping related reminders with a shared phrase, like "errands," so you can ask for the whole group at once. This tests whether Alexa keeps the group together. Check the results before you rely on it.

## Try it now

Pick one real errand you have this week. Say your Echo a single sentence that includes the task, the day and the time, for example: "Remind me to pick up [item] on [day] at [time]." Then open the Alexa app and check that it appears in your reminders list.
